transcript: We have to talk about the immersive theatre version of Stranger Things from 2020. And no, I'm not talking about this Instagram pop up experience, and I'm not talking about the Broadway play. I'm talking about the actual large scale immersive interactive theatre piece. I'm gonna tell you what it was like and how it worked. Welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback, where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history. First, you have to understand the context of the British company Secret Cinema, who you might recognize from the immersive Grease they did most recently. they did one for Star Wars, Blade Runner. I got to see the Moulin Rouge one, which was great. Their whole thing is that they do these large scale immersive experiences based around movies, and part of the concept is that the immersive theatre then culminates in a screening of that movie. Obviously they had to do something a little different with Stranger Things since it's a T V. show, which I'll talk about in a minute. Secret Cinema’s version of Stranger Things was based on season 3. The two central spaces they built were the Starcourt Mall, which had like a functional arcade, the ice cream shop and the 4th of July Carnival with actual food stands and games. But there were also a wide variety of peripheral spaces that you had to discover on your own. Like a great recreation of Hopper's cabin set in this creepy wooded area. At one point,I crawled through a tunnel to get to the secret lab or whatever. It was extremely fun. And aside from some spotty accent work from the British actors, the casting was shockingly on point. Like, look at Mike and Eleven here. It really felt like you were getting to interact with these characters that you know and love. How it worked narratively is that they basically ran through the plot of season 3 in about two and a half hours, which you might think is impossible, but remember, this is an immersive promenade show, so all of it is happening at the same time. And if you think about it, if it takes 8 hours of television to tell 4 or so parallel plot lines, then if you do them all at the same time, like a choose your own adventure, the math maths, that it would only take a couple hours. And speaking of choose your own adventure, I have to talk about the game-like mechanics in the experience. I think there were, like, 5 different paths that you could follow in the story, where you collaborate with the characters to gather information and complete tasks. And that element is where I personally had some frustrations with the experience. I saw a lot of story fragments, but I often got lost or hit dead ends, and there wasn't a ton of help from the performers to get back on track. So, logistically, that element I didn't love. Still though, it was pretty unforgettable, as was the cinema portion that took place after the main show. Essentially, instead of having us watch an episode of Stranger Things, they gathered us in the middle of this 360 degree space and played this multimedia montage of seasons 1-3, mostly from Eleven's perspective, weaving together key scenes from her central storyline, augmented by live practical effects and performers around the space. And this portion was an additional hour or so of the experience. It did feel a bit more like random and disjointed than it did with Secret Cinema's version of Moulin Rouge, where it really felt like the immersive theatre experience was culminating in the communal immersive screening. But the trade off was, I think the more theatre-centric portion of the show was more exciting and more fully-realized than it was in Moulin Rouge.
